rounds.proof_sketch: For input shape [16, 256, 256] with any dim ∈ {0,1,2}: grid.x = outer_size. CUDA guarantees blockIdx.x ∈ [0, gridDim.x-1] = [0, outer_size-1]. Therefore outer_idx = blockIdx.x can never equal outer_size. Both `outer_idx >= outer_size` and `outer_idx > outer_size` evaluate to FALSE for all reachable outer_idx values, making the mutation semantically equivalent.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the boundary guard from `outer_idx >= outer_size` to `outer_idx > outer_size`. This would only produce different behavior when outer_idx equals exactly outer_size. However, the kernel is launched with grid.x = outer_size, and CUDA guarantees that blockIdx.x ranges from 0 to gridDim.x - 1 (i.e., outer_size - 1). Since outer_idx = blockIdx.x, the value outer_idx = outer_size is architecturally impossible. Both the original and mutated conditions always evaluate to FALSE for all reachable thread indices, making them functionally identical regardless of input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation affects a boundary condition that can never be true given CUDA's grid/block indexing constraints. Killing this mutant would require changing how the kernel is launched (grid dimensions), which violates the fixed-shape contract.
rounds.recommendations: When writing boundary guards in GPU kernels, consider whether the condition can ever be true given the launch configuration. For mutation testing, guards that are architecturally unreachable (like checking blockIdx.x against gridDim.x when grid is sized to match) will produce equivalent mutants when boundary operators are modified. Consider either documenting these as accepted equivalent mutants or restructuring the guard to be more explicitly tied to the launch parameters.
